sections.title: The Definite Article ال
sections.rule: Arabic has one definite article, ال (al-), attached directly to the noun with no space and no separate word for 'a/an'. With the 14 'sun letters' the ل assimilates and the next consonant doubles; with the 14 'moon letters' the ل is pronounced clearly.
sections.example_ref: English: The book is on the desk. / The sun and the moon.
sections.note: al-kitāb (moon letter, l heard) vs ash-shams (sun letter, l assimilates). A bare noun with no ال is indefinite.

sections.title: Grammatical Gender
sections.rule: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine. The ending ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) usually marks the feminine, and adjectives must agree in gender with their noun.
sections.example_ref: English: The (male) student is diligent and the (female) student is diligent. / A new car.
sections.note: mujtahid → mujtahida. A few feminine words lack ة (أُمّ umm 'mother', شَمْس shams 'sun'); learn these as exceptions.

sections.title: The Dual Form
sections.rule: Arabic marks exactly two of something with a special dual suffix: ـانِ in the nominative and ـيْنِ in the accusative/genitive. Verbs and adjectives take dual forms too.
sections.example_ref: English: I have two new books. / The two students went to the library.
sections.note: kitāb → kitābān, ṭālib → ṭālibān. English has no dual; never use the plural for exactly two.

sections.title: The Past Tense (الماضي)
sections.rule: The past tense is built on the root following the base فَعَلَ. The he-form is the dictionary citation form; other persons add suffixes after it.
sections.example_ref: English: The boy wrote the lesson yesterday. / I wrote a letter and we wrote a report.
sections.note: kataba (he), katabat (she), katabta/-ti (you m/f), katabtu (I), katabnā (we). Only the ending changes.

sections.title: The Present Tense (المضارع)
sections.rule: The present/imperfect adds prefixes (and sometimes suffixes) to the root, following the يَفْعَلُ pattern. It expresses ongoing or habitual action.
sections.example_ref: English: The student writes every day. / I study Arabic and we learn together.
sections.note: ya- (he), ta- (she / you m.), a- (I), na- (we): yaktubu, taktubu, aktubu, naktubu. The prefix carries the person.

sections.title: Broken Plurals (جمع التكسير)
sections.rule: Most non-human nouns form irregular 'broken' plurals by changing the internal vowel pattern rather than adding an ending. There are many templates and each word is memorized.
sections.example_ref: English: One book and three books. / There are many houses in the neighborhood.
sections.note: kitāb → kutub, bayt → buyūt, walad → awlād, rajul → rijāl. Learn the plural with each new noun.

sections.title: Nominal and Verbal Sentences
sections.rule: A nominal sentence (الجملة الاسمية) starts with a noun and needs no verb for 'is/are' in the present. A verbal sentence (الجملة الفعلية) starts with the verb, giving verb–subject–object (VSO) order.
sections.example_ref: English: The weather is beautiful. / The boy went to school.
sections.note: aṭ-ṭaqs jamīl has no 'is'. In dhahaba al-walad the verb comes first and stays singular even before a plural subject.

sections.title: The Root System (الجذر)
sections.rule: Most Arabic words come from a three-consonant root that carries a core meaning. Fixed vowel-and-affix patterns wrapped around the root generate related nouns, verbs, and adjectives.
sections.example_ref: English: The writer wrote a book in the library. / The office is near the library.
sections.note: Root k-t-b (writing): kataba (wrote), kātib (writer), kitāb (book), maktaba (library), maktab (office). Spot the root to guess meaning.

sections.title: The Iḍāfa Construction
sections.rule: To show 'X of Y' or possession, two nouns are placed side by side. The first noun never takes ال or tanwīn; only the last noun may carry the article, and it is in the genitive case.
sections.example_ref: English: The door of the house is open. / The manager's car is in front of the office.
sections.note: bāb al-bayt = 'door (of) the-house'. Never write al-bāb al-bayt — the first term is made definite by position.

sections.title: Attached Possessive Pronouns
sections.rule: Possession is shown by a suffix on the noun instead of a separate word. The noun drops its own article when it takes the possessive suffix.
sections.example_ref: English: My book is on your desk. / Her house is near our house.
sections.note: -ī (my), -ka/-ki (your m/f), -hu/-hā (his/her), -nā (our), -kum (your pl.), -hum (their). kitāb-ī = 'book-my'.

sections.title: Sound Plurals
sections.rule: Regular ('sound') plurals of human nouns add ـونَ/ـينَ for masculine and ـات for feminine. The masculine form is ـونَ in the nominative and ـينَ elsewhere.
sections.example_ref: English: The (male) teachers are in the school. / The (female) teachers work hard.
sections.note: muʿallim → muʿallimūn/muʿallimīn; muʿallima → muʿallimāt. Sound plurals apply mainly to people and participles.

sections.title: Negation Across Tenses
sections.rule: The right negation particle depends on the tense: لا for the present, لم (+ jussive) for the past, لن (+ subjunctive) for the future, and ليس to negate a nominal sentence.
sections.example_ref: English: I do not know and I did not go. / I will not travel and the weather is not nice.
sections.note: lā + present, lam + jussive (lam adhhab), lan + subjunctive (lan usāfira), laysa 'is not'. Picking the right particle is key.

sections.title: Verb Forms (الأوزان)
sections.rule: From one root, derived patterns (Forms I–X) add predictable meaning: Form II فَعَّلَ is intensive/causative, Form III فاعَلَ reciprocal, Form X اسْتَفْعَلَ often 'to seek/use'.
sections.example_ref: English: The student studied, then he taught others. / The engineer used the new machine.
sections.note: darasa (studied, I) → darrasa (taught, II). istakhdama (X). The form tells you both the meaning and the vowels.

sections.title: Comparative and Superlative
sections.rule: The comparative uses the أَفْعَل pattern plus مِنْ ('than'). The same form made definite, or as the first term of an iḍāfa, gives the superlative.
sections.example_ref: English: This house is bigger than my house. / He is the tallest student in the class.
sections.note: kabīr → akbar, ṭawīl → aṭwal, jamīl → ajmal. akbar min = 'bigger than'; aṭwal ṭālib = 'tallest student'.

sections.title: The Future Tense (المستقبل)
sections.rule: The future is formed by prefixing سـ (near future) or the word سَوْفَ (further off) to the present-tense verb. Nothing else in the verb changes.
sections.example_ref: English: I will go to the market tomorrow. / We will study Arabic at the university.
sections.note: sa-adhhabu (I will go), sawfa nadrusu (we will study). sa- attaches; sawfa stands as a separate word.

sections.title: The Imperative (فعل الأمر)
sections.rule: The command form is built from the present stem by dropping the prefix and, when needed, adding a helping hamza. It matches the gender and number of the person addressed.
sections.example_ref: English: Write the lesson and read the book. / Go home and listen to what I say.
sections.note: uktub (write! m.), iqraʾ (read!), idhhab (go!), ismaʿ (listen!). Feminine adds -ī: uktubī. Negative command uses lā + jussive.

sections.title: Demonstratives: This and That
sections.rule: Demonstratives agree in gender and number. When the noun after them carries ال the phrase means 'this X'; without ال it makes a full sentence 'this is an X'.
sections.example_target_2: هٰذا الْكِتابُ جَديدٌ وتِلْكَ الْمَجَلّةُ قَديمةٌ.
sections.example_ref: English: This is a book and this is a magazine. / This book is new and that magazine is old.
sections.note: hādhā (this m.), hādhihi (this f.), dhālika (that m.), tilka (that f.), hāʾulāʾ (these), ulāʾika (those).

sections.title: Relative Pronouns (الاسم الموصول)
sections.rule: Relative pronouns like الَّذي/الَّتي agree in gender and number with their antecedent and are used only when the noun they refer back to is definite.
sections.example_ref: English: The man who lives here is a doctor. / The magazine that I read is useful.
sections.note: alladhī (m.), allatī (f.), alladhīna (m. pl.). With an indefinite noun no relative pronoun is used at all.

sections.title: كان and Its Sisters
sections.rule: كان and its 'sisters' (أصبح, صار, ظلّ, ليس …) enter a nominal sentence, keep the subject nominative, and put the predicate in the accusative case.
sections.example_ref: English: The student was diligent. / The weather became cold in winter.
sections.note: kāna al-ṭālibu (nom.) mujtahidan (acc. -an). The accusative predicate is the signature of this group.

sections.title: إنّ and Its Sisters
sections.rule: إنّ, أنّ, لكنّ, لأنّ, كأنّ, ليت, لعلّ introduce a nominal sentence, put the following subject noun in the accusative, and leave the predicate nominative.
sections.example_ref: English: Indeed God is forgiving, merciful. / I know that the student is diligent.
sections.note: inna Allāha (acc.) ghafūrun (nom.). Mirror image of kāna: here the subject, not the predicate, takes -a.

sections.title: The Verbal Noun (المصدر)
sections.rule: The maṣdar is an action noun ('the writing', 'the studying') derived from the verb. It commonly follows verbs like أراد and يجب and translates the English infinitive or -ing form.
sections.example_ref: English: I love reading books. / Studying is beneficial for the mind.
sections.note: kataba → kitāba, darasa → dirāsa, qaraʾa → qirāʾa. Form I maṣdars are least predictable — memorize them.

sections.title: Active and Passive Participles
sections.rule: The active participle (اسم الفاعل, فاعِل) names the doer and the passive participle (اسم المفعول, مَفْعول) names the thing done. Both function as nouns or adjectives.
sections.example_ref: English: The writer writes a carefully written letter. / The worker made something skillfully made.
sections.note: kātib (writer) vs maktūb (written); ʿāmil (worker) vs maʿmūl (made). Same root, opposite roles.
